scenes.heading: Lazy Evaluation
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Lazy Evaluation and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: How laziness works
scenes.narration: Lazy evaluation means that transformations like select, filter, and join do not run when you call them; they merely extend the logical plan. Nothing is computed until you invoke an action such as count, collect, or write. This deferral is deliberate, because seeing the whole plan at once is what lets Catalyst optimize it.

scenes.heading: Transformations vs actions

right.title: Actions (eager)
points: Return a value or side effect

scenes.narration: Transformations are lazy: they take a DataFrame and return a new one without doing work, extending the DAG. Actions are eager: they force Spark to execute the accumulated plan and produce a result or write output. Knowing which calls are which explains exactly when your job actually runs, and why an apparently slow line is really where an action fired.

scenes.code:
df = spark.read.parquet("/data/big")   # lazy
f = df.filter("amount > 0")            # lazy
s = f.select("user", "amount")          # lazy
# nothing has executed yet
print(s.count())                        # ACTION -> runs the whole plan
scenes.heading: Where execution really happens
scenes.narration: The read, filter, and select lines each return instantly because they only append to the plan. No data is touched during those three calls. Only when count is invoked does Spark build the DAG, optimize it, and run it end to end. Recognizing that the count line is where all the cost lives is essential for reading timings correctly.

scenes.text: Repeated actions recompute the plan unless you cache.
scenes.narration: Because laziness means each action replays the lineage, calling several actions on the same derived DataFrame recomputes it every time. Caching the reused DataFrame is the standard fix to avoid that repeated work.
